panels.figure_caption: Milky-creamy appearance of the case's plasma
in_text_mentions: A 20-day-old male patient was admitted to the emergency department for poor appetite and restlessness. He was exclusively breastfed. There was no fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. The patient was started on intravenous hydration and routine blood tests were performed. Venous blood gas showed the following results: pH: 7.41, PCO2: 40.7 mmHg, HCO3: 25.3 mmol/L, lactate: 2.2 mmol/L, and capillary glucose: 62 mg/dL. Other laboratory tests could not be evaluated because the patient's serum was extremely lipemic (Figure 1). The patient was admitted to the neonatal unit for careful monitoring.

in_text_mentions: She was admitted for further infectious disease evaluation. However, the diagnostic turning point came not from an advanced microbiological assay, but from a simple visual observation of her routine blood draws. Repeated samples were flagged by the laboratory for being profoundly lipemic - a finding initially dismissed as a post-prandial artefact. The key diagnostic step occurred when the clinical team visually inspected the spun serum tube, which revealed a thick, milky supernatant resembling strawberry cream (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single-image contrast-enhanced CT from FCS case report showing pancreatic sequelae of recurrent acute pancreatitis, a specific FCS complication. Caption provides pancreatitis manifestation; article title and in-text link to chylomicronemia syndrome with treatment-resistant triglycerides to 4,350 mg/dL. Mapped to acute_pancreatitis_ct vocabulary as chronic sequelae variant with chronic changes in proposed_findings.
panels.attribution_text: Berrocal et al. Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome Due to a Homozygous LPL c.644G>A Variant and Response to Volanesorsen in Colombia: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.111306. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, portal venous phase, coronal reconstruction. Yellow arrows indicate hypodense scar-like lesions within the pancreatic body and head, consistent with chronic sequelae of recurrent acute pancreatitis. The pancreatic parenchyma appears atrophic in the affected segments. No peripancreatic fluid collections or pseudocysts were identified.
in_text_mentions: emonstrated residual scar-like hypodense lesions in the pancreatic body, compatible with chronic sequelae of recurrent acute pancreatitis. Throughout this period, directly measured LDL and HDL cholesterol levels remained persistently low despite markedly elevated triglycerides, a pattern suggestive of an underlying chylomicronemia syndrome. Despite escalating combined treatment with statins, fibrates, and omega-3 fatty acids, triglyceride levels remained critically elevated, peaking at 4,350 mg/dL, demonstrating clear resistance to conventional lipid-lowering therapy (Table 1 and Figures 1-3).

in_text_mentions: girl initially presented a diagnostic conundrum with a one-year history of generalized, treatment-resistant papulovesicular rash. Born at term to consanguineous parents, she had otherwise been thriving with normal growth and development. Physical examination revealed multiple discrete vesiculopapular lesions distributed over her trunk, limbs, and groin, notably sparing the palms and soles (Figure 1). Given her age and the lesion morphology, infectious etiologies were primarily suspected, while classical lipid stigmata - such as eruptive xanthomas or xanthelasma - were not initially recognized.
